title: Review Comments on the Manuscript
overview: This manuscript investigates adaptive event-triggered H∞ control for interval type-2 (IT-2) fuzzy cyber-physical systems subject to stochastic deception attacks and Markov-type actuator failures. The combination of adaptive transmission and membership-function-derivative-dependent regional control is relevant to secure networked control. The numerical examples provide an initial illustration of the proposed framework. After reading, the primary features and contributions of this article are sound compared to some existing publications. However, the following aspects should be seriously considered to improve the presentation quality of this investigation.

items.comment: 1. The manuscript would benefit from careful language editing, particularly in the Abstract and Introduction. Some sentences combine several technical ideas, which makes the problem formulation and contributions harder to follow. Please review grammar, sentence structure, and the consistent use of abbreviations across the manuscript.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have revised the Abstract, Introduction, problem formulation, explanatory text in Section 3, numerical discussion, and Conclusion. The Abstract now proceeds from the attack/failure setting to the adaptive transmission and regional design, then to the sufficient conditions and numerical illustrations. We have corrected subject–verb agreement, removed a duplicated full stop and an unnecessary comma, clarified transitions, and made the terminology and abbreviations more consistent. In particular, the controller-gain description now refers to the gain for an individual fuzzy rule, and the distinction between an initial state in Example 2 and that of Example 1 is explicit. The detailed companion document records every implemented replacement, including punctuation and whitespace, rather than providing only selected examples. These changes improve exposition without modifying the displayed mathematical conditions or the numerical data.

items.comment: 2. The motivation for jointly considering deception attacks, actuator failures, and communication limitations needs clarification. These factors affect interconnected closed-loop components: attacks may corrupt sampled information, actuator failures may alter the effective control input, and event-triggered transmission limits unnecessary data exchange. Could the authors clarify why these factors require simultaneous consideration and how their combined effects influence closed-loop stability and H∞ performance?
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have added a paragraph following the actuator-failure discussion in the Introduction. It explains that deception attacks alter the information supplied to the controller, actuator failures alter the effectiveness of the input delivered to the plant, and event-triggered transmission retains the last transmitted sample between releases. The resulting sampling error, corrupted feedback, and actuator effectiveness enter the same closed-loop dynamics. Their coexistence therefore motivates evaluating stability and disturbance attenuation jointly under the specified models. This explanation identifies the coupling relevant to the control problem without suggesting that separate studies of the individual mechanisms are uninformative.

items.comment: 3. The Introduction cites several recent publications, but the relationship between the closest studies and the present contribution could be explained more explicitly. Please connect recent work on event-triggered control of IT-2 fuzzy systems, secure control under deception attacks, and actuator-failure compensation. Could the authors further clarify the methodological differences between the proposed approach and the most closely related studies? Please support these distinctions with the cited literature rather than simply adding references.
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have expanded the comparison immediately before the contribution list. Two directly relevant studies have been added: Liu, Ling, and Zhang (2025), on torus-event-based sliding-mode control of discrete-time IT-2 fuzzy systems under deception attacks, and Chandrasekar et al. (2026), on adaptive event-triggered asynchronous control of uncertain IT-2 fuzzy Markov jump systems with deception attacks. Their publication details and the methodological descriptions were checked against the publishers’ article pages. The comparison also explicitly cites the existing work by Chen et al. (2023) on probabilistic event-triggered control under cyberattacks and actuator failures. We distinguish the present continuous-time formulation, Markov-type actuator effectiveness, and derivative-sign-based regional synthesis. We also state that joint attack/failure modeling and adaptive event triggering are not, by themselves, claimed as new. The additions therefore strengthen positioning through concrete connections and distinctions, rather than citation count alone.

items.comment: 4. Remark 2.2 identifies the equilibrium value of the adaptive threshold, but its practical interpretation could be clearer. How do the adaptive threshold dynamics interact with the triggering condition and state error, particularly under different initial conditions? The discussion should avoid implying monotonic evolution for every initial condition and should not require changing the stated adaptive law.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have revised the sentence following the adaptive law and expanded Remark 2.2. The text now identifies 1/σ as the equilibrium threshold and distinguishes the two possible adjustment directions: with a positive threshold and nonzero error, the threshold increases below 1/σ and decreases above it. Its derivative is zero at equilibrium or when the triggering error is zero. We therefore do not assume that the threshold increases, or decreases, for every initial condition. We also explain that a larger threshold makes the triggering inequality harder to satisfy when the sampled state, error, and weighting matrix are held fixed. Actual release times still depend on their joint evolution. The triggering inequality and adaptive differential equation are unchanged.

items.comment: 5. The operational regions are determined by the signs of the membership-function derivatives. For readers unfamiliar with this construction, the link between a derivative sign pattern and the associated matrix constraints may not be immediately apparent. Could the authors explain how the signs of the membership-function derivatives determine the regional constraints and how these constraints are incorporated into controller synthesis? Please retain the existing theorem conditions and proof.
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have added an explanation after the regional-controller and triggering definitions in Section 2.4. Each derivative-sign pattern selects the matrix inequalities collected in its regional constraint set, and those inequalities are imposed together with the synthesis LMIs. The text gives a concrete example: a nonpositive membership derivative combined with a positive-semidefinite difference of the corresponding P matrices produces a negative-semidefinite derivative contribution; reversing both signs preserves this result. It separately explains why the R2 difference has the opposite orientation, in accordance with the existing nonnegative derivative requirement. The same choices are carried into the transformed synthesis conditions, after which the active sign pattern selects the regional gains and triggering matrix. No theorem condition, displayed equation, or mathematical derivation has been changed.

items.comment: 6. Table 1 reports packet counts and saving rates for several values of σ, but the implications of the trend could be discussed more explicitly. The reported packet count increases from 85 to 164 as σ rises from 4 to 20, while the saving rate decreases from 78.75% to 59.00%. Could the authors explain why the packet count increases and the saving rate decreases as σ rises, and how this trend relates to the adaptive threshold and triggering condition under the tested settings?
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have expanded the discussion after Table 1 and stated the time-triggered baseline of 400 candidate transmissions. The saving rate is defined as the fraction of baseline transmissions avoided. The text connects the reported increase from 85 to 164 packets, and decrease from 78.75% to 59.00%, to the decrease of the equilibrium threshold from 0.25 to 0.05 as σ increases from 4 to 20. For fixed sampled state, error, and weighting matrix, a smaller threshold makes the triggering condition easier to satisfy. We explicitly qualify this interpretation: the actual count also depends on the closed-loop trajectory, threshold dynamics, and resulting design matrices. Thus, the table documents the observed communication trade-off for these settings and is not presented as a universal monotonicity result. The entries in Table 1 have not been altered.

items.comment: 7. The manuscript derives sufficient conditions for stability and H∞ performance in terms of LMIs. The relationship between these two objectives could be explained more explicitly after the theorem statement. A brief interpretation would help readers distinguish the stability requirement from the disturbance-attenuation requirement; no change to the theorem or proof is requested.
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have added an explanatory paragraph immediately after Theorem 3.1 and its proof, before Remark 3.1. It maps the two objectives to Definition 2.1: stability concerns the unforced closed loop, whereas the prescribed H∞ level concerns the expected output-energy bound relative to disturbance energy for square-integrable disturbances under the definition’s zero-initial-condition convention. It identifies the output matrix C and performance parameter γ as the terms encoding the output–disturbance requirement in the same sufficient-condition framework. The paragraph also notes that infeasibility of these sufficient LMIs does not, by itself, establish instability. This is an interpretation of the stated result; the theorem conditions and derivation are retained.

title: Review Comments on the Manuscript
overview: The paper develops an adaptive event-triggered control strategy for IT-2 fuzzy CPSs in which the feedback channel may be subject to deception attacks and the actuators may switch among failure modes. This setting is relevant to networked implementations where information corruption, control-channel degradation, and communication limits may coexist. The manuscript is organized around a clear mathematical framework. The topic investigated in this manuscript is of interest, and the proposed control framework offers useful insights into the considered problem. However, several aspects require further clarification and discussion to strengthen the presentation of the results.

items.comment: 1. The literature review would benefit from more up-to-date coverage of secure control for IT-2 fuzzy cyber-physical systems, adaptive event-triggered control, and actuator-failure compensation. Could the authors include more recent, closely related studies to strengthen the research motivation and clarify the methodological distinctions and connections between this work and existing approaches?
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have expanded the comparison immediately before the contribution list. Two directly relevant studies have been added: Liu, Ling, and Zhang (2025), on torus-event-based sliding-mode control of discrete-time IT-2 fuzzy systems under deception attacks, and Chandrasekar et al. (2026), on adaptive event-triggered asynchronous control of uncertain IT-2 fuzzy Markov jump systems with deception attacks. Their publication details and the methodological descriptions were checked against the publishers’ article pages. The comparison also explicitly cites the existing work by Chen et al. (2023) on probabilistic event-triggered control under cyberattacks and actuator failures. We distinguish the present continuous-time formulation, Markov-type actuator effectiveness, and derivative-sign-based regional synthesis. We also state that joint attack/failure modeling and adaptive event triggering are not, by themselves, claimed as new. The additions therefore strengthen positioning through concrete connections and distinctions, rather than citation count alone.

items.comment: 2. Sections 2.3 and 2.4 introduce the deception signal and actuator-failure model separately. Could the authors clarify how the corrupted sampled state and actuator mode enter the control loop? Please add a concise bridging paragraph before the substitution leading to the closed-loop dynamics in Eq. (15).
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have inserted a bridging paragraph immediately before the substitution leading to Eq. (15). The paragraph follows the signal path: the attack model selects the transmitted state or its falsified replacement, the fuzzy controller acts on that received signal, and the actuator-effectiveness matrix acts on the resulting control input. We explicitly identify the resulting product with the plant input matrix in the closed-loop equation. The paragraph also explains that event triggering determines the release times and hence the sampled information retained between releases. This addition connects the separately introduced models to Eq. (15) without changing that equation or the underlying model.

items.comment: 3. Remark 3.1 introduces the two-sided FMF-dependent looped functional, but its motivation needs clarification. Although the control input is updated using sampled information, the system state evolves between sampling instants. Could the authors explain why this functional suits inter-sample behavior, how sampling-interval-dependent terms are incorporated, and why membership-function-related information is included? A concise explanation of these design choices and their benefits would clarify the theoretical framework.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have expanded Remark 3.1 by linking the functional components to their specific roles. The elapsed and remaining sampling-interval distances weight the two sides of the interval. The integral terms use state-derivative information before and after the current time, while the augmented vectors combine current and endpoint states with interval integrals. The endpoint matching of the auxiliary terms explains why they can represent intersample behavior within the looped-functional construction. The FMF-weighted matrices retain membership dependence, and the regional derivative constraints control the signs needed in the analysis. The threshold term connects the adaptation law to that analysis. We further clarify that future-endpoint quantities are analytical devices rather than additional measurements required by the implemented controller. The definition of the functional and its derivation remain unchanged; no quantified superiority over every alternative functional is claimed.

items.comment: 4. The proposed framework is developed for interval type-2 fuzzy systems. If the lower and upper membership functions coincide, how does the formulation reduce to the type-1 fuzzy case, and which features of the membership-derivative-dependent regional design remain applicable?
items.response:
Thank you for this insightful question. When the lower and upper membership functions coincide, the corresponding lower and upper firing strengths become identical. Since their weighting coefficients sum to one, the blended membership weight reduces to their common value under the normalization assumed in the model. Thus, the interval uncertainty disappears, and the model reduces to the type-1 fuzzy case.

However, the resulting membership functions may still vary with the system state, and their derivatives need not be zero. Therefore, the derivative-sign-based regional partition, regional controller gains, and associated matrix constraints remain applicable. These features exploit membership variation rather than interval uncertainty itself.

Accordingly, the existing stability and controller-synthesis conditions can be specialized to this type-1 case by substituting the corresponding membership functions, provided that the stated assumptions and LMI feasibility conditions remain satisfied.
items.response_only_note: 本条依据现有隶属函数表示及导数符号区域构造，解释区间二型退化为一型的特殊情形。不新增仿真或论文正文修改；充分条件的适用仍以现有假设及LMI可行为前提。

items.comment: 5. The manuscript needs careful language revision to improve grammar and logical flow. Several technical concepts appear in quick succession, particularly in the Abstract and Section 2. Please review sentence transitions, abbreviation consistency, and isolated grammar errors.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have revised the Abstract, Introduction, problem formulation, explanatory text in Section 3, numerical discussion, and Conclusion. The Abstract now proceeds from the attack/failure setting to the adaptive transmission and regional design, then to the sufficient conditions and numerical illustrations. We have corrected subject–verb agreement, removed a duplicated full stop and an unnecessary comma, clarified transitions, and made the terminology and abbreviations more consistent. In particular, the controller-gain description now refers to the gain for an individual fuzzy rule, and the distinction between an initial state in Example 2 and that of Example 1 is explicit. The detailed companion document records every implemented replacement, including punctuation and whitespace, rather than providing only selected examples. These changes improve exposition without modifying the displayed mathematical conditions or the numerical data.

items.comment: 6. The Conclusion should clearly distinguish current results from possible extensions. Could the authors state the underlying state-feedback and attack/fault assumptions and relate future work on output feedback or more general attack models to these assumptions? Please distinguish established results from directions that remain open.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have rewritten the final paragraph of the Conclusion to separate the scope of the current results from open directions. The current formulation is explicitly described as state feedback with Bernoulli-modeled deception attacks satisfying the stated signal bound and Markov-type actuator failures with known transition rates. The conclusions are qualified by these assumptions. Observer-based output feedback is identified as a future extension for applications without complete state measurements. DoS attacks and partially unknown transition rates are also identified as requiring additional modeling and analysis. These directions are not presented as results already established in this manuscript.

items.comment: 7. The framework involves both membership-derivative-dependent regional selection and Markov-type actuator-failure switching. Could the authors clarify the distinct roles of these two mechanisms and explain how they are jointly accounted for in the stability analysis?
items.response:
Thank you for this question. The two mechanisms have distinct roles. Regional selection is determined by the signs of the membership-function derivatives and determines the corresponding regional controller gains and matrix constraints. In contrast, Markov-type switching describes stochastic changes in actuator effectiveness through the actuator-failure modes and their transition rates. Thus, the regional index and the actuator-mode index represent different aspects of the system.

Both mechanisms are incorporated into the existing stability analysis. The regional constraints account for the membership-derivative terms in the functional derivative, while the Markov transition rates enter through the infinitesimal generator. The sufficient conditions are imposed for each actuator mode, fuzzy-rule combination, and regional constraint set. Therefore, the two mechanisms are considered jointly within the same stability framework.

title: Review Comments on the Manuscript
overview: This study addresses adaptive event-triggered H∞ control for IT-2 fuzzy CPSs affected by stochastic deception attacks and actuator failures. Its technical route combines an adaptive triggering law, regional conditions based on membership-function derivatives, and LMI-based analysis. The numerical section contains a PMSM case and a second fuzzy-system example. The topic investigated in this manuscript is of interest, and the proposed control framework offers useful insights into the considered problem. However, several aspects require further clarification and discussion to strengthen the presentation of the results.

items.comment: 1. The manuscript requires further editing to improve English grammar, sentence structure, and readability. Some expressions are informal or awkwardly phrased, particularly in the Abstract and Introduction. Careful language polishing is recommended to ensure clear and consistent academic expression.
items.response: Thank you for this comment. We have revised the Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusion to improve academic tone, precision, and consistency. The Abstract now presents the problem, method, sufficient conditions, and numerical illustrations in a clearer order. General expressions have been replaced with descriptions of the specific mechanisms; for example, the discussion of fixed thresholds now states that they do not adjust online to the relevant fluctuations. We have also corrected grammatical errors and clarified abbreviations. The Conclusion describes the numerical results as illustrations under the selected settings and states the assumptions of the analysis, avoiding claims that go beyond the established results.
items.revision_plan: 改摘要、引言和结论的语言，不改公式。将泛泛、口语化的评价改为具体技术描述；统一术语和缩写；将数值结果表述为所选条件下的展示。详细版逐项列出实际措辞和标点改动。

items.comment: 2. Why is it necessary to consider deception attacks, actuator failures, and communication limitations together? The Introduction should explain their interaction in the feedback loop more clearly and strengthen the practical motivation for the proposed framework.
items.response: Thank you for this question. We have added a motivation paragraph explaining the roles of the three factors in the feedback loop. Deception attacks can corrupt the sampled information used by the controller, while actuator failures alter the effectiveness of the resulting control input. Event-triggered transmission retains the last transmitted sample between releases, so the controller also operates with a sampling error. The plant therefore evolves under a control action influenced simultaneously by the available sample, possible data corruption, and actuator effectiveness. The added paragraph explains why these interacting effects motivate a joint stability and disturbance-attenuation analysis under the specified models.
items.revision_plan: 在引言的执行器故障讨论之后补一段联合研究动机，按“采样信息被篡改—控制作用受故障影响—两次传输间保留旧样本”的闭环关系说明三者的联系。沿用现有模型，不追加新模型或仿真。

items.comment: 3. The interpretation of the adaptive-threshold parameter in Remark 2.2 is not sufficiently clear. Please explain its relationship with the equilibrium threshold and how the threshold evolves from different initial values under the influence of the sampling error.
items.response: Thank you for this question. We have clarified the interpretation of the existing adaptation law in Remark 2.2. For a positive threshold and nonzero sampling error, the threshold increases when it is below 1/sigma and decreases when it is above 1/sigma. Its derivative is zero when the error is zero or the threshold equals 1/sigma. The weighted error magnitude scales the rate of adjustment. For fixed sampled state, error, and weighting matrix, a larger threshold makes the triggering inequality harder to satisfy. We also explain that actual transmission times depend on the joint evolution of these quantities, so the equilibrium alone does not imply the same trajectory or communication savings for every initial condition.
items.revision_plan: 修正参数sigma的解释，并扩充Remark 2.2，分别说明初始阈值位于平衡值上方、下方及误差为零时的情况，再联系触发不等式。保留原自适应律，不改公式，也不把特定仿真趋势说成普遍保证。

items.comment: 4. The manuscript employs a two-sided looped functional incorporating fuzzy membership information. Could the authors explain how the looped structure captures inter-sample dynamics and what additional benefits the membership-dependent terms bring to the stability analysis?
items.response: Thank you for this question. The two-sided looped structure uses the elapsed and remaining parts of a sampling interval, together with state and state-derivative information, to describe evolution between sampling instants. The auxiliary looped terms satisfy the endpoint-matching property used in the analysis, allowing this inter-sample information to enter the functional framework. Membership dependence provides complementary information: the weighted matrices retain the active fuzzy memberships, and their derivatives involve membership-function derivatives. The regional constraints exploit the signs of these derivatives in the stability and synthesis conditions. We have expanded Remark 3.1 to explain these roles separately and then their combination. This explanation identifies the information used by the construction without claiming an unverified quantitative advantage over all alternative functionals.
items.revision_plan: 扩充Remark 3.1：先解释已过去/剩余采样时间、V2/V3/V4中的状态与积分项以及端点匹配，再解释隶属函数加权矩阵和导数符号约束的作用。说明分析中的未来端点量不是控制器所需的额外测量，不新增保守性比较实验。

items.comment: 5. The connection between the membership-function derivatives and the regional matrix constraints needs further explanation. How do the derivative signs determine the directions of the matrix inequalities? A representative example would help readers understand the regional controller design.
items.response: Thank you for this suggestion. We have added an explanation after the regional controller and triggering definitions in Remark 2.4. For example, a nonpositive membership-function derivative multiplied by a positive semidefinite matrix difference gives a negative semidefinite term; for a positive derivative, reversing the matrix inequality produces the same sign. We also explain why the R2-related inequality has the opposite orientation, as the analysis requires a nonnegative derivative for that weighted matrix. Collecting these choices gives the constraint set for each region, which is imposed together with the synthesis LMIs. This addition explains the existing constraints without altering the theorem or proof.

Third, "condition … guarantee" in the proof of Theorem 3.1 should read "condition … guarantees". Please correct these errors and check the manuscript for similar issues.
items.response: Thank you for identifying these errors. We have corrected the saving rate in Example 2 from 83.79% to 83.75%, using (1 - 65/400) × 100%. The reported transmission count and candidate-sample count remain unchanged. In Section 2.4, the description has been revised to "where K_n denotes the controller gain for rule n". In the proof of Theorem 3.1, "condition … guarantee" has been corrected to "condition … guarantees". We have also checked the saving rates in Table 1 against the reported counts; all four are consistent with the same calculation. These corrections do not change the simulation data, controller matrices, theorem conditions, or proof arguments.
